title: Thermal bar
summary: A fixed aluminium bar heated uniformly — no mechanical load at all, just thermal strain against a restraint.

steps.title: Choose display units
steps.explain: Millimetres suit a small bar like this one.

steps.title: Add the bar
steps.explain: A thin, long fin: 120 mm long, 20 mm wide, only 3 mm thick.

steps.title: Define the material, with alpha
steps.explain: `material.add` takes `alpha`, the coefficient of thermal expansion, alongside `E` and `nu` — without it, `load.temperature` has nothing to convert a temperature change into. `k` (conductivity) is here too, though only a heat-transfer Step would use it.

steps.title: Assign it
steps.explain: Link the Material to the bar.

steps.title: Mesh it
steps.explain: A lattice mesh at 5 mm — plenty for a thin bar in uniform temperature.

steps.title: Fix the root
steps.explain: Without a restraint, a uniformly heated bar just grows freely and carries no stress at all — the restraint is what turns thermal expansion into a stress. Fix one end.

steps.title: Heat it
steps.explain: `load.temperature` sets a uniform temperature on one or more Bodies relative to `reference` (default 293.15 K). There is no mechanical load in this Model at all — the temperature change is the only load.

steps.title: Add a Step
steps.explain: One static Step, with the restraint and the heat load active together.

steps.title: Thermal strain
steps.explain: A free (unrestrained) temperature change produces strain with no stress at all; restraining even part of that strain is what produces stress. That is the whole of thermal loading — no new physics, just alpha times delta T fed into the same stiffness the mechanical loads use.
steps.theory:
Free thermal strain: epsilon = alpha * delta_T (no stress, if nothing restrains it).
Here alpha = 2.3e-5 /K and delta_T = 60 K, so the unrestrained strain would be epsilon = 1.38e-3 (0.138 %).
Fixing one end converts the restrained fraction of that strain into stress via the usual sigma = E * epsilon.
